amadan.story: Come. The two stems barely resemble each other: past umad-, present ā-, which sounds like yā- after mi- or bi-. Persian shouts “umadam!” (literally “I came!”) to mean “Coming!”, as if it has already arrived. “Khosh umadi” (welcome) is literally “you came well.”

imperative.en: come!
come! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t come!
don’t come! (polite, or to more than one)

raftan.story: Go. In the present, the stem rav- shrinks to a single r: miram, I go. In the command, be- becomes bo- because the o in ro pulls the vowel toward itself: boro. Persian likes its vowels to rhyme. The stem makes nouns too: piyāde-ro, the “foot-goer,” is a sidewalk.

imperative.en: go!
go! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t go!
don’t go! (polite, or to more than one)

shodan.story: Become. The busiest verb in the house: it turns an adjective into an event. Boland (tall) + shodan gives “get up,” literally “become tall.” Bidār (awake) + shodan gives “wake up.” Only shodan changes; the adjective stays put. One collision to watch: nashin can mean “don’t become” (to a group) and also “don’t sit.” Context decides.

get up! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t get up!
don’t get up! (polite, or to more than one)
wake up!
wake up! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t wake up!
don’t wake up! (polite, or to more than one)

neshastan.story: Sit. Spoken Tehrani swallows the first syllable of the present stem: mineshinam becomes mishinam. The stem also makes people: shahr-neshin (city-sitter) is a city dweller, and ruz-neshin, the “day-sitter,” is a person stuck at home.

sit! (polite, or to more than one)
don’t sit!
don’t sit! (polite, or to more than one)

stems.present: hidden in the endings (-am, -i, -e…), or bāsh- for commands

budan.story: Be. A cousin of English “be,” from the same ancient root. In the present it hides: the endings do the work, so khubam means “I’m fine.” It shows itself in the past (budam, I was) and borrows its own word for “not” (nistam, I’m not). To someone who has been working, Persians say “khaste nabāshi”: may you not be tired.

kardan.story: Do, make. Same ancient root as the Sanskrit karma. Persian builds verbs from it like Lego: sabr (patience) + kardan is “wait,” ajale (haste) + kardan is “hurry,” negāh (a look) + kardan is “look.” In these compounds the command usually drops bo-: sabr kon, not sabr bokon.

didan.story: See. Past did-, present bin-, and that bin is everywhere: durbin (far-seer) is a camera, khoshbin (good-seer) an optimist, badbin (bad-seer) a pessimist. And “didi?!” (did you see?!) is the gossip’s favorite word.

khordan.story: Eat. Persians also eat water and tea: āb khordan, chāy khordan. Here the command keeps its bo-, because breakfast and tea are things being eaten, not part of the verb: sobhune bokhor!
